cards.name: OS-eDRAM: IGZO/IWO 2T0C gain-cell memory IP on a U.S. 200mm foundry
cards.what_it_is: Replace '~4-5x the bit density of 130nm SRAM' with '~2-4x the bit density of 130nm SRAM'
cards.why_it_could_work: IGZO off-current ~3e-19 A/um gives >400-1,000 s retention (imec IEDM 2020/2021) vs SRAM's constant leakage, so an always-on edge chip can hold weights/activations at near-zero standby power. A planar 2T0C at ~30F2 is ~0.5 um2/bit at 130nm vs ~2.0-2.5 um2 for 6T SRAM [ESTIMATE], and because it sits in BEOL it uses no extra silicon area. Arbitrage: SkyWater bought Fab 25 (~$73M + working capital, ~400k wafer starts/yr) and is converting it to a foundry, so it needs differentiated process options. Embedded-memory IP royalties carry ~85% gross margin.

cards.name: Standalone IGZO 2T0C DRAM die on a depreciated U.S. 200mm line (commodity DRAM substitute)
cards.what_it_is: Build discrete DRAM-substitute chips (DDR4/LPDDR-class interface) from four stacked IGZO 2T0C tiers over CMOS periphery on a depreciated U.S. 200mm 130nm line (SkyWater Fab 25 Austin) and sell them into the 2026 shortage. A capacitor-less, BEOL-stackable cell on cheap wafers is the whole pitch.
cards.why_it_could_work: No capacitor, low-temperature BEOL, and stackable tiers (IMECAS showed 4-layer 3D 2T0C with 400 s retention and 3 bits/cell at VLSI 2026), with depreciated 200mm wafers at ~$1-2.5K [ESTIMATE], while DDR5 sells for ~$27/GB. The scratch model kills it: ~0.0035 Gb/mm2 => ~7.6 GB per 200mm wafer => ~$336/GB including test and packaging, ~12x today's DDR5 price, ~31x the glut price and ~125x DDR5's estimated cost (~$2.7/GB). Even a hypothetical 300mm 28nm-class 4-tier version models at ~$11.8/GB, about the glut price and ~4x DRAM cost, and no U.S. foundry offers that line.

cards.name: IGZO memory printed on idle display-fab glass
cards.what_it_is: Use a depreciated Gen 6-8.5 oxide-TFT display backplane line (the CAAC-IGZO process Sharp and SEL commercialized) to pattern 2T0C memory arrays on glass, then cut and bond them to silicon sense/IO chips as cheap bulk memory. Large-area tooling and a 4-6 mask process are the 'cheaper process/capital' bet.
cards.why_it_could_work: Display oxide-TFT lines are heavily depreciated and running underutilized (Omdia 2025). IGZO TFT leakage is tiny (SEL CAAC-IGZO <=200 zA), and a Gen 8.5 sheet is ~5.5 m2. Scratch model: at a ~2 um design rule a 2T0C cell is ~120 um2 => ~4e-6 Gb/mm2 => only ~2.3 GB per sheet => ~$266/GB before bonding, with microsecond access.

cards.name: U.S.-made HZO FeRAM family (1-16 Mb, rad-hard option) via SkyWater + Sandia
cards.what_it_is: A fabless company designs a family of hafnium-zirconium-oxide 1T1C FeRAM chips (SPI/QSPI and parallel, 1-16 Mb, plus rad-hard variants). The HZO capacitor module would be built on SkyWater's 130nm line (Bloomington MN or Fab 25 Austin), with rad-hard variants co-developed with or licensed from Sandia, which integrated HZO FeRAM into its trusted MESA fab at 200mm (May 2026). It sells an onshore second source to Infineon's PZT F-RAM.
cards.why_it_could_work: HZO is ALD-deposited and CMOS-friendly (no PZT lead contamination; ~2-3 extra masks, by analogy to TI's 2-mask FRAM on 130nm) and radiation hard (heavy-ion data; Sandia program). Space/defense F-RAM is close to sole-source (Infineon QML-V 2Mb). Wafers: ~$1,400 per 200mm [ESTIMATE]. This is a supply-security play, not a $/GB play: the scratch model is ~$770/GB because these are Mb-class parts.

cards.name: AlScN ferro-diode memory for 500-600C electronics (Penn/AFRL license + STTR)
cards.what_it_is: License Penn's AlScN ferroelectric-diode NVM (Jariwala/Olsson group, co-developed with AFRL) and build kB-to-Mb memory dies and high-temperature packaged modules for SiC electronics. Target uses are hypersonics, turbine-engine health monitoring, downhole geothermal/oil tools and Venus/space probes, entered through AFRL/DARPA SBIR-STTR contracts.
cards.why_it_could_work: Silicon DRAM and flash fail well below 300C [ESTIMATE]. Ni/Al0.68Sc0.32N/Pt diodes switched at 600C for >60 h at <15 V, which is compatible with SiC logic (Nature Electronics 2024), and scaled devices reach >100 Mbit/mm2 (arXiv 2025). The 2-terminal self-rectifying crossbar is a simple 3-4 mask BEOL. DoD keeps asking for this: AF254-D0806 (500C kB-scale NVM manufacturing scale-up) and DARPA DPA26BZ04-DV017 (-269 to +600C NVM, ~$1.2M Direct-to-Phase II, closed Aug 2026).

cards.name: 3D XPoint / PCM Crosspoint Revival for the CXL Memory Tier
cards.what_it_is: Rebuild Optane-class memory: Ge-Sb-Te phase-change (or OTS selector-only) cells in a 4-deck 20nm-half-pitch crosspoint, sold as CXL Type-3 persistent/capacity memory at a fraction of DRAM $/GB during the shortage.
cards.why_it_could_work: The math looks great in Nov-2026: XPoint Gen2 was 1.31 Gb/mm2 (~3.3x 1b DRAM density) and at full fab loading the die cost computes to ~$1/GB vs DDR5 at ~$20/GB. But Optane died anyway: Intel lost >$7B, took a $559M inventory write-off (Q2-2022); Micron cited 'insufficient market validation', booked ~$545M underutilization in 4 quarters and sold Lehi to TI for $900M (below book). The killers were volume (Lehi underloaded), an Intel-only DDR-T ecosystem, ~3-4x DRAM latency, and the 2019 DRAM glut erasing Optane's ~$6.6/GB price advantage. SanDisk + imec are now prototyping '3D Matrix Memory' (target ~half DRAM cost/bit, no dates).

cards.name: Optane PMem Salvage: Cheap Memory-Mode Capacity for Cascade/Ice Lake Fleets
cards.what_it_is: Buy decommissioned Intel Optane PMem 100/200 modules (128/256/512 GB, 3D XPoint Gen1 media) from U.S. ITAD/recyclers, health-test them (ipmctl SMART/percentage-used, burn-in), and sell validated kits plus a web sizing tool that configures Memory Mode or App Direct for VMware/KVM, SAP HANA, Redis and HPC nodes on 2nd/3rd-gen Xeon Scalable servers.
cards.why_it_could_work: DDR4 RDIMMs rose >50% QoQ in Q3-2026 and DDR4 is being exited, so owners of still-useful Cascade Lake/Ice Lake fleets cannot cheaply add memory. New PMem cost $6.6-11/GB in 2019 and Intel exited with ~2 years of excess XPoint inventory; recovered modules may trade at ~$0.8-2/GB [UNVERIFIED] vs DDR4 RDIMM ~$25+/GB. Memory Mode uses DRAM as cache in front of 4-8x more PMem capacity. Software (sizing, health certificates, config scripts) is the founder's edge.

cards.name: Thyristor RAM revival (T-RAM TCCT / Kilopass VLT)
cards.what_it_is: Revive the thin capacitively-coupled thyristor (TCCT) T-RAM cell, or Kilopass's vertical-layered-thyristor (VLT) cross-point cell, as a capacitor-less SRAM/DRAM replacement on a U.S. line (a GF U.S. SOI flow or SkyWater 90nm FD-SOI [UNVERIFIED-training]). cards.why_it_could_work: A PNPN latch stores the bit with built-in gain, so it reads fast (1-2 ns claimed) and needs no capacitor. The earliest Stanford NDR-cell patents (~1998) have expired, so IP is no longer the barrier [UNVERIFIED-training].

cards.name: Si gain-cell eDRAM (GCRAM) IP for U.S. trailing-node SoCs
cards.subbranch: Capacitor-less silicon DRAM: 2T/3T gain-cell eDRAM in logic
cards.what_it_is: A memory-IP company that builds and licenses a logic-compatible (zero extra masks) 2T/3T silicon gain-cell eDRAM compiler, first for SkyWater S130/S90 FD-SOI and GlobalFoundries 12LP+ (Malta NY). It replaces 6T SRAM in edge-AI activation buffers, image-sensor line buffers and FPGA block RAM. Revenue is a per-node license fee plus royalty, sold through the foundry IP catalog, as SkyWater already does for Weebit ReRAM.
cards.why_it_could_work: SRAM scaling has stalled. 6T SRAM silicon costs ~$55-72/GB at 7-28nm, ~$195/GB at 65nm and ~$1,330/GB at SkyWater 130nm (01_LANDSCAPE s4.4), so a gain cell at ~50-60% of 6T area saves ~40% of memory area. Foundries pay for differentiated embedded memory (GF-RAAAM 2026; SkyWater-Weebit).

cards.name: OpenRAM macro service for U.S. open-PDK tapeouts (SkyWater S130)

cards.what_it_is: A software-first business that generates, DRC/LVS-verifies, silicon-characterizes and supports SRAM macros (later gain-cell macros) for teams taping out on SkyWater S130 (Bloomington, MN) through ChipFoundry shuttles. It is built on the BSD-licensed OpenRAM compiler and sold as a SaaS subscription (hosted macro generator, characterized Liberty/LEF/GDS libraries, CI regression) plus per-tapeout support, listed on the ChipFoundry Marketplace.
cards.why_it_could_work: OpenRAM is alive (v1.2.50, 2026-10-27), but only 1-4 KB prebuilt sky130 macros exist. They are periphery-dominated: a 2 KB macro takes 0.2845 mm2 (57.6 kbit/mm2), ~6x worse than the 1.896 um2 bitcell allows. Small teams cannot afford commercial memory compilers ($50k-$200k+ per node [UNVERIFIED-training]). ChipFoundry runs an IP marketplace on an active SkyWater shuttle flow. The work is Python, CI and web tooling, which is the founder's skill set.

cards.name: Cryo-CMOS gain-cell eDRAM IP for quantum-computer control
cards.what_it_is: A memory-IP and test-chip business offering Si gain-cell eDRAM macros characterized at 4 K and 77 K for cryo-CMOS qubit-controller ASICs, fabbed on GF 12LP+ (Malta NY) or SkyWater 90nm FD-SOI. Revenue is NRE plus licenses from quantum hardware teams and national-lab programs.
cards.why_it_could_work: At cryogenic temperatures subthreshold leakage collapses, so Si gain-cell retention rises from microseconds to seconds or more [UNVERIFIED-training]. That makes refresh nearly free while keeping ~2x SRAM density and very low static power. This matters because the 4 K stage has only ~1 W of cooling budget. Superconducting memories (SFQ/JMRAM) remain far less dense.

cards.name: DDR4 Second-Life CXL Expander
cards.subbranch: CXL memory expansion / DIMM reuse (Microsoft-Meta style DDR4 recycling)
cards.what_it_is: A PCIe Gen5 x16 CXL 2.0 Type-3 add-in card or 1U 'JBOM' holding 8-12 decommissioned DDR4-3200 RDIMMs behind a merchant DDR4-capable CXL controller (Marvell Structera X 2404-class or Microchip SMC 2000-class). A U.S. EMS (e.g. Sanmina) assembles it, and it ships with burn-in and qualification to operators moving to DDR5-only Xeon 6 / EPYC 9005 servers. The process 'materials' are DRAM that is already fabbed and paid for, and the capital is DIMMs that are already depreciated.
cards.why_it_could_work: Reuse beats buying DDR5 for any owner at used-RDIMM resale values, not only at hyperscaler scale. Card $2.34/GB plus recovered DDR4 $4-11/GB = $6.3-13.3/GB against a $20.31/GB DDR5 RDIMM (4Q26 canonical), a +$7-14/GB advantage. In the glut it is $2.84-3.84 against $8.12, a +$4.3-5.3/GB advantage. Structera X 2404 runs 12 DDR4-3200 DIMMs (3 DPC) with inline LZ4 (sampling since Q4 2024).

cards.name: KV Pool Node (shared DRAM+CXL KV-cache appliance)
cards.subbranch: LLM inference KV-cache tiering - DRAM/CXL tier
cards.what_it_is: A 2U EPYC 9005 / Xeon 6 server (Supermicro or Dell OEM chassis) holding 3-6 TB of DDR5 plus E3.S CXL memory modules (Samsung CMM-D, Micron CZ122 or SK hynix CMM-DDR5), with 2x400G RDMA NICs. It ships with Mooncake Store / LMCache MP preconfigured to allocate KV on the CXL tier (/dev/dax). It is sold as a rack-shared 'KV memory node' that pools prefix and agent-session caches across GPU servers running vLLM/SGLang/Dynamo.
cards.why_it_could_work: KV is large: Llama-3.1-70B is 320 KiB/token at BF16 (40 GiB per 128k context); DeepSeek-V3 MLA is 68.6 KiB/token. Reloading a 128k context (20 GiB FP8) over 400G RDMA takes ~0.5 s, against ~41 s to recompute on one H100. Holding KV in DDR5 pays if a prefix is reused at least once every ~1.35 h at 4Q26 prices (~3.4 h in the glut). Mooncake reports 75% more requests within SLO at Kimi. vLLM requires the CPU tier as the staging tier, and LMCache/Mooncake already speak CXL /dev/dax.

cards.name: Memory-Fabric SuperNIC (Ethernet-attached DRAM for GPUs) - acquired away
cards.subbranch: Far memory over RDMA / custom memory-fabric silicon
cards.what_it_is: A custom NIC/switch ASIC that attaches pools of commodity DDR5 (behind CXL controllers) to GPU servers over 800G-3.2T Ethernet/RDMA, giving each GPU tens of TB of 'elastic' memory for KV cache and weights. This is the Enfabrica ACF-S/EMFASYS concept, taped out at TSMC.
cards.why_it_could_work: GPUs need far more memory than HBM supplies (KV for a 128k Llama-70B context is 40 GiB at BF16). Ethernet/RDMA reloads a 128k context in ~0.5 s vs ~41 s recompute, and commodity DDR5 at ~$26/GB beats HBM-in-GPU at ~$180-250/GB.

cards.verify_reason: The statute and its date are confirmed. FAR Case 2023-008 was proposed in the Federal Register on 2026-02-17, takes effect 2027-12-23 and covers SMIC, CXMT and YMTC plus products that incorporate their chips. Comments closed 2026-04-20, and no final rule was found (via search snippets). But the card's fatal flaw has largely materialized. The proposed rule is a certification (52.240-XX/-YY) after a 'reasonable inquiry', with no third-party audit, no affirmative duty to prove compliance, and a safe harbor for reasonable reliance on supplier certifications under 5949(h). cards.name: Memory FinOps Audit for Cloud SaaS
cards.what_it_is: A read-only web app with an AWS IAM role. It reads CUR plus CloudWatch-agent/Prometheus memory metrics across EC2 r/x/m-family, ElastiCache, RDS, K8s pods and JVM heaps. Output is a fixed-fee 'memory diet' report and a monitoring subscription, sold through AWS Marketplace to 20-500-engineer SaaS companies. The playbook levers are r->m family downsizing, K8s in-place pod resize (stable v1.35), JDK compact object headers and Redis->Valkey.
cards.why_it_could_work: AWS list prices put marginal RAM at $2.56-2.62/GiB-month, and RAM is 28-43% of the m7i/r7i list price (computed). Clusters leave about 18% of memory unused (Sysdig via KRR). Take a $40k/month EC2 bill with RAM at 30%, of which half the unused 18% is realizable: that saves about $1.1k/month, so a 25% share-of-savings fee is about $270/month. Reaching $20k MRR needs about 74 customers (d_calcs.py in D_notes).

cards.name: Fleet Memory-Reclaim Autopilot (TMO for on-prem)
cards.subbranch: Transparent memory compression / proactive reclaim / dedup
cards.what_it_is: A per-node agent plus web control plane. It enables and tunes upstream Linux zswap (zsmalloc + zstd/lz4), Meta-Senpai-style PSI-driven proactive reclaim via cgroup2, KSM page dedup on Proxmox/KVM hosts, and Kubernetes 1.34 LimitedSwap, with per-workload SLO guardrails and a 'GB reclaimed = $ of DRAM not bought' ledger. It is sold per node to on-prem/colo operators who buy DRAM at 2026 prices.
cards.why_it_could_work: On-prem buyers pay for DRAM directly: DDR5 RDIMMs cost $14-16/GB at contract and ~$32/GB street, and used 64GB DDR4 RDIMMs cost $250-370 ($3.9-5.8/GB, amcompute 12-month data to Aug-2026). Take a 200-server x 512GB fleet with 20% cold memory at ~2:1 compression: it frees ~10 TB. That defers $154k (DDR5 contract) to $328k (DDR5 street) of purchases, but only ~$40-59k on a DDR4 fleet topped up with used DIMMs. Kubernetes container swap went GA in v1.34. Meta's TMO saves 20-32% of total memory fleet-wide (ASPLOS 2022, confirmed via snippet). Hetzner's 2026 price increases (up to 37% from Apr-1, citing RAM/NVMe) show hosting providers feel the cost.

cards.name: KV-Cache Tier Integration & Tuning for Self-Hosted LLMs

It deploys host-DRAM and NVMe KV-cache tiers (LMCache, NVIDIA Dynamo KVBM, Mooncake Store, SGLang HiCache) into mid-market vLLM/SGLang clusters and sizes the DRAM tier per workload from measured prefix-reuse rates. cards.name: DIMM Health Subscription: predictive replacement + recovered-DDR4 spares pool
cards.subbranch: SaaS + spares pool (third-party maintenance for memory only)
cards.what_it_is: A per-node agent built on the open-source rasdaemon/Linux EDAC stack streams corrected and uncorrected DRAM error counts per DIMM to a web console. It flags DIMMs trending toward failure (row/page corrected-error growth) and triggers next-business-day shipment of a burn-in-tested replacement from a spares pool of recovered DDR4 RDIMMs bought from U.S. R2 ITADs (Iron Mountain/ITRenew-Sesame, Sims, regional R2 firms). It sells at ~$0.75 per DIMM-month to operators keeping out-of-warranty Dell R740/HPE DL380 Gen10-class DDR4 fleets alive because 2026 DRAM and server prices make a refresh unaffordable.
cards.why_it_could_work: High DRAM prices push enterprises, universities, regional colos and MSPs to stretch DDR4 server life: DDR4 contract prices rose 24% in the 3 months to Oct 2026, and a 64GB RDIMM went from $450 to >$900 on contract. Out-of-warranty fleets lose OEM DIMM replacement. Telemetry is free (rasdaemon logs CE/UE events to SQL and already supports per-page/per-row CE thresholds), so the product is integration plus logistics. Model (e_estimates §10): a 2,400-DIMM customer pays $21.6k/yr. COGS is $8.9k at 2026 recovered-DDR4 prices (58.6% GM) and $3.9k in a glut (81.9% GM), because spares get cheaper. The pool needs only ~$7k of capital per customer. 25 customers = $540k ARR.

cards.name: Memory Cost Escalation Index + EPA clause kit
cards.what_it_is: Publish a monthly, methodology-documented memory cost index family (DDR4, DDR5, LPDDR4X/5X, eMMC/NAND). It is computed from authorized-distributor quote APIs (Nexar/Octopart, DigiKey, Mouser) plus transaction data contributed by a marketplace partner such as Mobius Materials. License it with ready-to-use economic-price-adjustment (EPA) clauses and a calculator API, so system integrators, EMS houses and federal contractors can pass memory cost through in both directions, like steel and copper surcharges. Federal contracts already allow index-based material EPA (FAR 16.203-1(a)(3), FAR 52.216-4).
cards.why_it_could_work: Memory moved about 6x on contract in five quarters (index 100 -> 601) and will probably fall ~60% in 2028-29. Fixed-price deals for servers, industrial PCs and embedded systems either bleed or carry fat contingencies; Samsung's own device division lost money on component costs in 3Q26. A neutral index lets both sides drop the contingency. Example (e_estimates §11): memory is 35% of a $500k deliverable, so +25% memory triggers a +$43.75k adjustment and -60% a -$105k refund. Revenue: 30 x $6k + 5 x $24k = $300k ARR at 89% GM if self-built, 57% if a contract-price feed must be licensed.

The card misses a federal adoption barrier. cards.name: Authorized-aftermarket die bank for EOL legacy DRAM (title-taking LTB aggregator)
cards.what_it_is: Become a DFARS-recognized authorized aftermarket manufacturer/authorized supplier for EOL legacy DRAM (DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4) from a Taiwanese specialty maker (Winbond, ESMT, Etron or Nanya). Buy last-time-buy wafer lots, bank die in nitrogen at an East Coast site, and package and test on demand at U.S. OSATs (Micross Apopka FL / RTP NC, QP Technologies) for defense, avionics, rail and medical OEMs that need the parts for 10-20 years. Unlike C-61, a consignment vault for OEM-owned stock, this takes title and holds OCM authorization.
cards.why_it_could_work: DFARS 252.246-7008 and 246.870-2 make DoD contractors buy from OCMs, authorized suppliers or authorized aftermarket manufacturers before anyone else, so OCM authorization is a regulatory moat. DDR4 EOL pain is documented: Advantech steering customers off Samsung DDR4, and zero authorized stock of a Micron DDR4 part in May 2026. Model (e_estimates §5): a $600k single-part bank returns 16% IRR in the base case (sold at 3.0x die cost, 90% sold in years 3-8), -7% in the bear case and 39% in the bull case. Unit GM is 33-66%.

cards.glut_reason: Demand is driven by EOL and requalification cost, not DDR5 prices, and a glut cheapens LTB wafers. The main risk is inventory that never sells (bear IRR -7%).

Rochester already holds >10B banked die, 70+ OCM authorizations and a legacy-DRAM partnership with Intelligent Memory, so it is the firm OCMs call first. A startup can neither win the authorization nor fund $0.6M per part ($2M+ for a portfolio). Without authorization the venture is just an independent distributor, which DFARS ranks last.

cards.name: CXL memory-tiering integration practice (consulting -> managed tuning)
cards.what_it_is: A services firm that assesses, deploys and tunes CXL Type-3 memory expansion and tiering on Granite Rapids/Turin servers. Hardware: Micron CZ-series, Samsung CMM-D or SK hynix CMM expanders, and Marvell Structera- or Astera Leo-based cards. Software: Linux weighted-interleave and DAMON tiering, SK hynix HMSDK. Clients are HPC centers, in-memory database hosts and EDA shops, and engagements convert into a managed tuning and monitoring subscription.
cards.why_it_could_work: 1 TB of new DDR5 RDIMM costs ~$20.8k per node at 4Q26 prices (e_estimates §12). CXL lets buyers add cheaper or reused capacity, including DDR4 behind Structera-class controllers, without buying top-bin DIMMs. Mainline Linux still has CXL gaps (Dynamic Capacity, multi-host sharing), so integration know-how is scarce. Practice revenue: ~$83k/yr part-time, ~$248k full-time at $225/h.

cards.name: Memory patent expiry and litigation radar
cards.what_it_is: A subscription web app that tracks memory-relevant U.S. patents (DRAM module/PMIC, MRAM, ReRAM, FeRAM, IGZO, 3D DRAM). It computes expiry dates (term adjustments, terminal disclaimers, maintenance-fee lapses), follows assignment changes and PTAB/ITC/district-court dockets (e.g., ITC 337-TA-1487 Avalanche v. Everspin; the Netlist RDIMM/PMIC cases), and provides FTO checklists per product type. It is built from free USPTO bulk data plus PACER/ITC EDIS.
cards.why_it_could_work: Every hardware concept in this study has an FTO gate: Netlist PMIC for DDR5 modules, SEL for IGZO, the ITC case for Everspin STT. One FTO opinion costs $10-30k and NPE defense $0.6-4M (p1-ip). Everspin spent $6.0M on litigation in one quarter. Small module makers, recert firms and memory startups need cheap monitoring. 25 subscribers x $4.8k = $120k ARR at ~85% GM.
